Hypothesis: In HCC, hyperactivated AR signaling upregulates HK2 expression, thereby enhancing aerobic glycolysis which creates an acidic, immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment that drives resistance to sorafenib. Utilizing state-of-the-art genomic and metabolomic profiling, a subset of HCC patients characterized by this AR/HK2 hyperactivation can be identified. In these patients, a combined therapeutic strategy employing next-generation AR and HK2 inhibitors—implemented through advanced techniques such as CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing and RNA interference—along with sorafenib treatment is hypothesized to disrupt glycolytic reprogramming, reduce tumor growth, and overcome drug resistance. Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) often exhibits varied mechanisms of therapeutic resistance, including metabolic reprogramming that supports tumor survival. Our revised hypothesis posits that in a molecularly defined subset of HCC, hyperactivation of androgen receptor (AR) signaling directly upregulates hexokinase 2 (HK2), thereby enhancing aerobic glycolysis. This heightened glycolytic flux leads to an acidic and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment that facilitates sorafenib resistance. By leveraging modern genomic and metabolomic profiling alongside cutting‐edge CRISPR/Cas9 and RNA interference technologies, patients with an aberrant AR/HK2 axis can be identified and selectively targeted. We propose that combined inhibition of AR and HK2, in tandem with sorafenib, will reduce glycolytic flux, diminish acidification, promote cancer cell apoptosis, and ultimately overcome drug resistance, while also monitoring compensatory pathways such as HGF/c-Met signaling.
Orignal_vs_New: The revised hypothesis retains the original causal chain: AR activation upregulates HK2 expression, which enhances aerobic glycolysis, establishes an acidic microenvironment, and contributes to sorafenib resistance; inhibition of AR and HK2 then reverses these effects. However, the new hypothesis incorporates contemporary technological capabilities by proposing the use of genomic and metabolomic profiling for patient stratification and advanced therapeutic techniques (e.g., CRISPR/Cas9 and RNA interference) to precisely target the AR/HK2 axis. Additionally, it acknowledges the role of alternative pathways such as HGF/c-Met, providing a more comprehensive and practically implementable approach to overcoming sorafenib resistance in HCC.
